newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Catalan debt auction said successful.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Catalan debt auction said successful.

text.p: The first bond auction by Spain's Catalan regional government on Wednesday was hailed as a success after the spread over Bonos narrowed, dealers said.
The 10-year bonds were the most sought after and the spread over Bonos slimmed to 13 basis points from between 20 and 25.
That could lead the Generalitat of Catalunya to increase its future offers in this segment, the Generalitat's financial director Xavier Ruiz del Portal told Reuters.
"If the good demand for 10-year bonds is confirmed, we could increase the amount offered in 10-year bonds," he said.
The next auctions are on November 20 and December 18.

Five-year notes maturing July 18, 2001, with a coupon of 8.10 percent, drew bids for 37.215 billion pesetas and were allotted for 4.75 billion pesetas. The minimum price was set at 106.00 while marginal yield was 7.136 percent.

Ten-year bonds maturing July 18, 2006 with an 8.85 percent coupon received bids for 40.70 billion pesetas, with an allocation of 4.5 billion. The lowest price was set at 108.70 and the maximum yield was 7.905 percent.

The allocation resulted in a spread over Bonos of 13 basis points for the 10-year bonds and of 17 points in the five-year paper. Under the old system of direct allocation, the average spread was 20 to 25 basis points in the 10-year segment.
That compares to five-year Bonos due April 2001 which were trading at 105.31 to yield 6.962 percent and 10-year Bonos due April 2006 at 106.67 yielding 7.76 percent.
On Wednesday, market conditions were not ideal, dealers said. At 1245 GMT the futures contract was down 47 basis points at 107.00.
Also Libor market conditions limited foreign investors' participation, especially in the five-year segment.
"The spread over Bonos is higher in five-year than in 10-year bonds, but also the spread over Libor is wider in the shorter term," said a dealer in Madrid.
That explains the limited participation in the five-year auction by foreign investors, who usually finance their positions at Libor, dealers explained.

The new system of monthly auctions set up by the Generalitat of Catalunya is expected to provide the autonomous region with a more efficient way to sell its debt on the market. But the old direct system of private placement will also remain in use.
In absolute terms, Catalonia has the highest level of debt among the 17 Spanish regional governments, 1.018 trillion pesetas at the end of June 1996.
Catalonia is considered one of the richest regions in Spain and its debt is still one of the highest in relative terms.

A recent study published by the Confederacion Espanola de Cajas de Ahorro showed that as a ratio to gross domestic product, Catalan debt rose to 7.3 percent at the end of 1995 from 3.6 percent in 1992. These values were respectively at 5.7 percent at 3.6 percent for the whole of Spain.
Moody's rating for Catalan debt stands at A1, while Sandard & Poor's is AA-minus.
